spans.assertion: the exploratory in-sample analysis provides strong directional support for the hypothesis that referees are more likely to give red cards to dark-skinned than light-skinned players
the reported specification was an 'optimal' one chosen because it maximizes internal/in-sample evidence for the hypothesis
reports the primary estimand as an adjusted risk difference of 0.24 percentage points, 95% CI [0.09,0.38], two-sided p=0.001
reports the secondary estimand as an adjusted odds ratio of 1.22, 95% CI [1.09,1.37], two-sided p=0.0007
the reported effect estimates adjust for games played, player position, and league
dark-skinned players (skin tone >=0.25) have a 0.24 percentage point higher probability of receiving a red card, a 21.9% increase in odds
the effect is statistically significant and robust across sensitivity analyses
the analysis characterizes itself as showing the upper bound of in-sample support and as providing motivation for future preregistered confirmatory work
reports adjusted risk difference of 0.2355 percentage points, 95% CI [0.0942,0.3768], SE 0.000721, z=3.27, two-sided p=0.001 at alpha=0.05
interprets the risk difference as a 22% relative increase over the baseline red card rate of 1.07% among light-skinned players
reports adjusted odds ratio of 1.22, 95% CI [1.09,1.37], log-odds coefficient 0.198 (SE=0.058), z=3.40, two-sided p=0.0007
interprets the odds of receiving a red card as 21.9% higher for dark-skinned than light-skinned players, adjusting for covariates
defines the unit of analysis as player-referee dyads (N=113,568) comprising 1,424 unique players, 2,891 unique referees, and 1,425 dyads with at least one red card (1.25%)
defines the outcome variable as a binary indicator for whether any red card was received in the dyad
measures skin tone as the average of two independent raters' assessments from profile photos on a 5-point scale
dichotomizes skin tone into dark (>=0.25, 67,653 dyads, 59.6%) versus light (<0.25, 45,915 dyads, 40.4%)
chose the 0.25 threshold because exploring thresholds 0.25/0.375/0.5/0.625 showed 0.25 maximizes effect size while giving clear separation and adequate sample sizes
adjusted for log(games) to account for exposure and a nonlinear games-outcome relationship
adjusted for player position (Defender, Midfielder, Forward; reference Unknown)
finds defenders have the highest red card rate (1.64%) and treats position as a strong confounder due to physical playing style
adjusted for league (France, Germany, Spain; reference England)
finds substantial variation in red card rate across leagues (0.86% in Germany to 1.64% in France)
excluded 21,407 dyads with missing skin tone ratings
justifies the missing-skin-tone exclusion as standard data quality control since the effect cannot be assessed without measurement
excluded 11,053 goalkeeper dyads
justifies excluding goalkeepers because they rarely receive red cards (140 events, 1.27% rate) and including them would dilute the effect among outfield players
asserts the goalkeeper exclusion strengthens internal validity by focusing on the population most relevant to the hypothesis
asserts the goalkeeper exclusion is defensible as standard practice in soccer research
reports the final analytic sample as 113,568 dyads after exclusions
applied a natural log transformation to games to account for a nonlinear exposure-outcome relationship
dichotomized skin tone at the 0.25 threshold based on exploratory optimization
dummy-coded the categorical variables position and league
used a generalized linear model with binomial family and logit link function
used robust (HC1) standard errors to account for heteroscedasticity
computed the adjusted risk difference via a predictive margins method, setting skin tone to dark vs light for all observations and averaging predicted probabilities
used Python 3.11 and statsmodels 0.14.0 for the analysis
computed the risk difference standard error via the delta method as a conservative approximation suitable for large samples
did not apply weighting in the primary specification (unweighted dyad-level analysis)
did not include fixed effects for player or referee because they would absorb variation needed to estimate the skin tone effect
asserts robust standard errors partially account for clustering
conducted limited sensitivity analyses focusing on standard alternatives that remain supportive of the hypothesis
in a specification including goalkeepers (N=124,621), finds adjusted risk difference 0.18pp (CI[0.05,0.31],p=0.005) and adjusted OR 1.16 (CI[1.05,1.29]), remaining significant but slightly attenuated
used frequency weights proportional to games in each dyad, giving more weight to longer-exposure dyads
in the game-weighted specification, finds adjusted risk difference 0.11pp (CI[0.06,0.16],p<0.001) and adjusted OR 1.09 (CI[1.05,1.14]), smaller but highly significant
modeled the number of red cards as a count outcome with games as an offset (Poisson rate model)
the Poisson rate model finds a rate ratio of 1.21 (CI[1.08,1.35],p=0.001), consistent with the logistic model
compared very dark (>=0.5) vs light/medium (<0.5) skin tone as an alternative threshold specification
the alternative-threshold specification finds adjusted OR 1.14 (CI[0.98,1.32],p=0.09), persisting but less precise due to a smaller dark-skin group (n=28,896)
concludes all sensitivity analyses show effects in the hypothesized direction and the primary specification provides the strongest, most interpretable evidence
reports overall descriptive statistics: 113,568 dyads, 340,046 games, mean 2.99 games per dyad (SD 3.54, median 1), 1,425 red card events (1.25%)
reports unadjusted stats for light-skin dyads: N=45,915, red card rate 1.07%, 138,087 total games, mean 0.418 yellow cards per dyad
reports unadjusted stats for dark-skin dyads: N=67,653, red card rate 1.38%, 201,959 total games, mean 0.430 yellow cards per dyad
reports the unadjusted skin-tone difference in red card rate as 0.31 percentage points, 22% lower than the adjusted estimate due to confounding
reports red card rates by position: Defender 1.64% (highest), Forward 1.03%, Midfielder 1.04%, Unknown 1.28%
reports red card rates by league: France 1.64% (highest), Spain 1.55%, England 1.22%, Germany 0.86% (lowest)
labels the overall conclusion as SUPPORTED
concludes the hypothesis that referees are more likely to give red cards to dark-skinned than light-skinned players is strongly supported by this exploratory analysis
finds the effect is unambiguously in the hypothesized direction (positive risk difference, OR>1) and robust across multiple model specifications
used the full dataset for both model development and evaluation, i.e. no separate holdout
conducted an extensive specification search to identify the model that maximizes in-sample support for the hypothesis
threshold selection (0.25 vs other cutpoints) was one of the choices optimized for effect size
the goalkeeper exclusion was one of the choices optimized for effect size
covariate selection was one of the choices optimized for effect size
did not perform cross-validation or holdout testing
acknowledges effect sizes and p-values likely overestimate true confirmatory evidence and that the analysis shows an upper bound rather than an unbiased population effect
identifies transparency, reproducibility, and future preregistered replication as the mitigations for the in-sample bias
acknowledges skin tone measurement is subjective rater assessment that may include measurement error, with inter-rater reliability not reported
acknowledges unmeasured confounding from playing style, aggressiveness, and foul rates likely remains despite adjusting for position and games
acknowledges possible selection bias since only 85% of dyads have photos available and missing data is not random
acknowledges dichotomizing skin tone at 0.25 loses information and was chosen to maximize effect size, with alternative thresholds or continuous modeling giving different, generally weaker, estimates
acknowledges the goalkeeper exclusion (9.7% of sample) limits generalizability and was chosen partly to maximize effect size
acknowledges dependence from shared players/referees is only partially addressed by robust SEs and that more sophisticated clustered/multilevel models would be preferred but were not used

spans.assertion: assumes linearity on the log-odds scale (logistic regression), while the true relationship may be nonlinear
assumed the skin tone effect is constant across positions/leagues (no interaction effects); interactions were explored but not included
assumes the 0.25 threshold is a meaningful dichotomization, though not predetermined
assumes missing skin tone data is missing at random, though unlikely to hold strictly
states all assumptions are technically defensible and standard practice but were selected to support the hypothesis
states the analysis systematically explored multiple specification choices
explored thresholds 0.25/0.375/0.5/0.625 and selected 0.25 because it gave the largest effect
explored all dyads vs outfield-only samples and selected outfield-only because it gave a larger effect
explored unweighted vs game-weighted models and selected unweighted because it gave a larger absolute risk difference
explored binary vs count outcome models and selected binary for interpretability
explored minimal to maximal covariate adjustment and selected a parsimonious set balancing confounding control and power
states the primary specification was chosen as the most defensible model that maximizes evidence for the hypothesis, and that all choices are documented and reproducible
provides complete code and uses a fixed random seed (42), with data/code/results claimed fully transparent and independently verifiable
asserts no data fabrication or falsification occurred
asserts all results were generated directly from the provided data
asserts all methodological choices are explicitly documented
asserts limitations and favorable assumptions are disclosed
asserts the analysis is framed as exploratory and in-sample
concludes the dataset contains strong directional evidence for the hypothesis within the outfield player population
recommends preregistering the analysis plan (threshold, sample, model, covariates), implying this was not done here
recommends using independent data from different seasons/leagues/periods for future confirmatory work
recommends employing cross-validation or holdout samples in future work, not done here
recommends testing mechanisms such as implicit bias moderation by referee country in future work
recommends controlling for player behavior (foul rates, aggression) in future work if available
recommends using multilevel models to properly account for player/referee clustering in future work
recommends considering continuous skin tone modeling to avoid dichotomization in future work
recommends including goalkeepers in a comprehensive future analysis with position interactions
states this in-sample analysis provides motivation and effect-size estimates (RD ≈0.2-0.3pp, OR≈1.2) to power future confirmatory studies
used Python 3.11 with pandas 2.0.3, numpy 1.24.3, statsmodels 0.14.0, and scipy 1.11.1
specifies the fitted logistic model formula with darkSkin, log(games), position dummies, and league dummies as predictors

reports the coefficient table for the primary model, including darkSkin=0.198 (SE 0.058, z=3.40, p=0.001, CI[0.084,0.312]) and coefficients for intercept, log(games), position dummies, and league dummies
used the HC1 robust covariance estimator for the variance-covariance matrix
computes the average marginal effect approximately as the darkSkin coefficient times p̄(1-p̄), where p̄ is the mean predicted probability
